title: Electrochemical Reduction of CO2 to Methanol over MWCNTs Impregnated with Cu2O
abstract: This study evaluated the reduction of CO2 to methanol in the presence of effective and stable MWCNTs impregnated with Cu2O. A preliminary DFT study shows that the incorporation of Cu2O in MWCNTs improves the electronic properties of the electrocatalyst. The surface morphology and structural interaction between Cu2O and MWCNTs at different Cu2O loadings (10-50 wt %) were characterized by SEM, TEM, EDX, XRD, BET, TGA, and Raman spectroscopy. Characterization results show that the Cu2O particles are incorporated at defect sites in the MWCNT matrix. However, higher lodgings (40 and 50 wt %) result in the agglomeration of Cu2O particles and crystallite size growth. Electrochemical evaluation of the catalyst for CO2 reduction was conducted in a two-component polycarbonate electrochemical cell. Linear sweep voltammetry results show that the 30% Cu2O-MWCNTs catalyst gives the highest current density in the entire potential range, and a faradaic efficiency of 38% was achieved at -0.8 V for the reduction of CO2 to methanol. The study shows that the impregnation of Cu2O on MWCNTs affects the structural and electronic properties of the electrode, which in turn improves both the activity and stability of the catalyst as confirmed by chronoamperometry.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Prior to the increase of industrial activity in the late 60s, the concentration of CO2 in the atmosphere was about 350 ppm [1], [2]. However, rapid industrialization and population growth
drastically increased the CO2 concentration to 398 ppm, recorded in 2015 [3]. The average temperature on earth will significantly increase if CO2 concentration rises to 550 ppm, which is an alarming situation leading to the disruption of our eco-environment [4]. As the excessive
dependence on fossil fuels has both depleted the fossil fuel reserves and significantly increased
the atmospheric CO2 concentration, renewable energy is now considered as an attractive alternative to fossil fuels [5], [6].
Carbon dioxide has been reduced on a commercial scale to methanol and other hydrocarbons
using the hydrogenation process. This process is not that efficient due to the high temperature
and pressure together with the large amount of hydrogen required [7]. A range of photocatalysts
has also been used for the photochemical reduction of CO2. However, the electron/hole recombination and the limited intensity of light affects the efficiency of photochemical
production of hydrocarbons and methanol [8], [9].
Electrochemical reduction of CO2 is an attractive route for the conversion of CO2 to useful products at room temperature and pressure. A variety of reduction products such as methanol,
formic acid, methane, and CO have been formed using both aqueous and non-aqueous systems
[10]–[12]. During the period from 1960 to 1980, CO2 was electrochemically reduced using amalgams of copper, zinc, and mercury. These amalgamated electrodes formed formic acid as
the major CO2 reduction product [13], [14]. However, Frese and coworkers showed for the first
time in the 1980s that methanol can be formed as the main CO2 reduction product using ruthenium and molybdenum based catalysts, albeit at a low current density of 1 mA-cm -2 [15]–
[17]. In the mid-eighties Hori et al. [18]–[21] investigated the reduction of CO2 on copper foil, which produce ethylene and methane. The work of Hori et al. was a promising step towards
using copper based electrodes for CO2 reduction. They also tested electrodes made of Ni, Pd, Au, Zn, and Ag, which were able to reduce CO2 to CO. However, Cu was found to be the best material for the reduction of CO2 to methane. Electrodes made of Cd, Sn, Pb, In, and Hg formed formic acid as the main product [22]. Electrodes based on Pt, Fe, Rh, Mo, and Ti perform poorly
in the reduction of CO2 due to the high hydrogen evolution [18]–[21]. Many metal oxides of Group IV to Group X metals exhibit a very low rate of reduction, producing mainly hydrogen
during reduction [23]–[26]. On the other hand, Cu (I) species in Cu2O directly reduces CO2 to methanol by electron trapping due to the high adsorption energy of CO2 [27]–[31].
The main challenge in the electrochemical CO2 reduction process is the prevention of the reduction of water at the cathode. The reduction potential of water is very close to the reduction
potential of CO2:

The low current density, the low overpotential for H2O reduction, and the low product selectivity are the major problems faced in the electrochemical reduction of CO2. Therefore, an electrocatalyst that has a high overpotential for the reduction of H2O and allows more H + (protons) to be exchanged is required for the reduction of CO2 to useful hydrocarbons [32]–[34].
Multi wall carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) possess excellent structural and electrical properties,
which make them strong candidates for electrochemical applications [35]. Functionalized
MWCNTs have good electrical conductivity, a mesoporous and microporous structure with
uniform and straight pores, and good acid and base resistance. Low mass transfer resistance of
MWCNTs increases the residence time of adsorbates in the pores, making them attractive to be
used as supports in a variety of applications [36]. In addition, functionalized MWCNTs have a
tubular structure with a high length-to-diameter ratio (aspect ratio), enabling the pores to behave
as molecular wires for electron transfer between the electrode and CO2 in the electrolyte solution [35]. The electrocatalytic activity, chemical stability, modifiable surface, and unique morphology
of the MWCNTs make them well suited to be used as supports for Cu2O electrocatalysts.
In this study, functionalized MWCNTs impregnated with varying amounts of cuprous oxide
were investigated for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to methanol. The experimental work was preceded by a computer simulation study using the density functional theory (DFT) and time
dependent DFT quantum mechanical techniques to simulate the properties of the semiconductor
electrocatalyst. The surface and structural properties of the electrocatalyst were determined using
a range of techniques including scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron
microscopy (TEM), energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX), X-ray diffraction (XRD),
Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) surface area measurement, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA),
and Raman spectroscopy. The properties of the electrocatalyst with varying compositions were
then correlated to the electrochemical performance of the electrodes. Several electrochemical
techniques were used to evaluate the performance of the electrocatalyst based on Cu2OMWCNTs for CO2 reduction. Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) was used to measure the current density of Cu2O-MWCNTs with varying Cu loadings. Chronoamperometry (CA) was used to calculate the faradaic efficiency (FE), which provides an indication of the amount of methanol
produced at different potentials for Cu2O-MWCNTs with optimized Cu2O loadings. Stability of the electrodes was also evaluated using chronoamperometry.

sections.heading: 2. DFT Simulation
sections.text:
The density functional theory (DFT) and time dependent DFT quantum mechanical techniques
were used to simulate the structure of the proposed electrocatalyst to determine the improvement
in the electronic properties due to surface modification of the MWCNTs by Cu2O. All the DFT calculations were performed using Amsterdam Density Functional (ADF) program (2013.01).
BAND mode was used to simulate the Cu2O and the Cu2O-MWCNTs structures. The crystal structure with a single layer surface slab was selected. All atoms were mapped within the unit
cell to accurately optimize the geometry of the crystals. The Cu2O and the Cu2O-MWCNTs models were simulated using the hybrid TZ2P (triple-zeta double-polarized) basis function. In all
calculations, the relativistic effects were taken into account by the zero order regular
approximation (ZORA) Hamiltonian in its scalar approximation [37][38].
The Cu2O and Cu2O-MWCNTs geometries were optimized using the Hartree-Fock model and triple-ζ polarization basis function. The optimized structures of Cu2O and Cu2O-MWCNTs are shown in Fig. 1. Incorporation of MWCNTs in the Cu2O structure reduces the band gap from 2.10 to 1.78. The reduction increases the electron flow to the conduction band which favors the
adsorption of intermediates, resulting in high current densities with high stability and selectivity
towards methanol formation.
Fig. 1. Optmized structures: (a) Cuprous oxide (Cu2O) and (b) Cu2O-MWCNTs obtained using DFT simulation
3. Materials and Methods
3.1 Materials
All reagents were of analytical grade and were used as received. The dimensions and properties
of the MWCNTs purchased from the Cheap Tubes Corporation (USA) are as follows: outer
diameter 10-20 nm, inner diameter 5-10 nm, length 10-30 µm, purity ˃95%, and specific surface area (SSA) ˃138 m 2 /g. Millipore deionized (DI) ultrapure water (18 MΩ .cm) was used to
prepare all aqueous solutions. Copper (II) chloride (CuCl2. 2 H2O, A.R. grade, ≥ 99.0%), sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS, C.P. grade, ≥ 85.0%), hydroxylamine hydrochloride (NH2OH.HCL, A.R. grade ≥ 98.5%), sodium hydroxide (NaOH), and isopropanol were purchased from (Sigma-
Aldrich). Carbon dioxide gas with purity of 99.999% was purchased from the SIGAS Company.

3.2 Preparation of the Cu2O-MWCNTs Electrocatalyst

sections.heading: 3.2.1 Functionalization of the MWCNTs
sections.text:
The MWCNTs were functionalized with carboxyl groups (COOH) using nitric acid to enhance
the properties of the MWCNTs. One gram of carbon nanotubes was sonicated in 75 ml of concentrated HNO3 for 30 min and then heated at 120 o C for 48 h with vigorous stirring [39]– [41]. The mixture was allowed to cool to room temperature and washed with deionized water 5
times in a centrifuge (CR22GIII, Hitachi) at 12000 rpm. Then, the functionalized MWCNTs were dried and placed in a vacuum oven at 85 o C for 12 hours. The attachment of COOH groups
to the surface of the MWCNTs was confirmed by FTIR characterization of the functionalized
samples.

sections.heading: 3.2.2 Impregnation of the functionalized MWCNTs with Cu2O
sections.text:
The functionalized MWCNTs were impregnated with Cu2O by adding the desired amount (for a loading from 10 to 50%) of copper chloride salt (0.1 M CuCl2 light blue) and 0.1 g of sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) to an MWCNTs suspension under vigorous stirring. The suspension of the
MWCNTs was prepared by sonicating 1 g of the functionalized MWCNTs in 500 ml of
deionized water for 30 minutes to attain a good dispersion. The suspension of the MWCNTs containing Cu ions was then placed in a water bath at 30 o C and allowed the temperature to
equilibrate. The desired amount of sodium hydroxide (1.0 M NaOH) was then added and the
color of the solution changed to yellowish green, confirming the presence of copper(II)
hydroxide (Cu(OH)2). Hydroxylamine hydrochloride (0.1 M NH2OH.HCL) was then introduced rapidly to the yellowish-green MWCNTs suspension, and stirred for 30 min to allow nanocrystal
growth. Finally, the suspension was centrifuged at a speed of 4500 rpm for 5 minutes with deionized water to obtain the pure catalyst, which was then dried in vacuum at 75 o C for 12 h.
3.3 Fabrication of the Electrodes and Electrochemical Measurements
Several electrochemical techniques were used to evaluate the performance of the Cu2OMWCNTs electrocatalyst in the CO2 reduction. Linear sweep voltammetry was used to measure the current density of Cu2O-MWCNTs at several Cu loadings, and chronoamperometry was used to calculate the faradaic efficiency. The faradaic efficiency gives an indication of the changes in
methanol formation at different potentials for Cu2O-MWCNTs at optimized Cu2O loadings. Stability was also evaluated using chronoamperometry. All electrochemical measurements were
performed in a polycarbonate electrochemical cell with two compartments separated by a nafion
membrane. Fig. 2 shows the three-electrode system containing a Cu-foil working electrode, a
platinum (Pt) counter electrode, and a Ag/AgCl reference electrode. The surface of the copper
foil was cleaned and polished using sand paper prior to applying the catalyst. An ink was
prepared by sonicating the electrocatalyst with 0.8 ml of a 5% nafion solution in isopropanol for
30 min. The ink was then brushed on the cleaned and polished Cu foil and was allowed to dry to
make the working electrode. Prior to each experiment, nitrogen was bubbled for 20 minutes
through the electrolyte to remove air. Then, CO2 with a purity of 99.999% was bubbled for 20 minutes through the 0.5 M NaHCO3 electrolyte. First, the electrochemical behavior of a blank copper foil electrode was studied in the electrolyte with and without bubbling CO2 through it. Then the electrochemical behavior of the functionalized MWCNTs and MWCNTs with different
loadings of the catalyst (10%, 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50% of Cu2O) was studied. After each experiment, the organic deposition on the nafion membrane was cleaned by immersing it in 10% HNO3 at 80 o C for two hours and washing with deionized water to remove any acid residues.
Fig. 2. The polycarbonate electrochemical cell with two compartments separated by a nafion membrane
3.4 Characterization of the Cu2O-MWCNTs Electrocatalyst Surface and structural properties of the electorcatalyst with a varying composition were
determined using a range of characterization techniques. The structural and surface properties
were correlated with the electrochemical performance of the electrode and used to optimize the
Cu2O loading on the MWCNTs. The surface area of the catalysts was determined by the BET method using a Micromeritics model ASAP 2000 analyzer, using physical adsorption of liquid
N2 at 77K. The surface morphology was studied using a scanning electron microscope (SEM - JEOL JSM-646OLV), combined with an energy dispersive X-ray (EDX) spectrometer, which
was used to determine the elemental composition of the samples. The phase composition and
crystal size of the electrocatalysts were determined by XRD. The samples were characterized using a Rigaku XRD X-ray diffractometer with Cu-Kα radiation and 2θ in the range of 20 o -80 o at a scan rate of 0.02 o min -1 . The crystallographic orientation of Cu2O on the surface of the MWCNTs was determined by Raman spectroscopy. A LabRam GR evolution system provided
by HORIBA instruments was used to conduct the Raman spectroscopic characterization. A
transmission electron microscope (TEM - FETEM JEOL, JEM-2100F) was used to determine
the dispersion of Cu2O on the surface of the MWCNTs, along with their particle size. Thermal stability of the catalyst was determined by TGA using an SDT Q600 analyzer from TA
Instruments.
4. Results and Discussion
4.1 SEM-EDX Analysis
Fig. 3 (a) shows the existence of strong binding between the functionalized MWCNTs and
Cu2O. The SEM images (Fig. 3 (a) and (b)) of the electrocatalyst with 10% and 30% loadings indicate that the Cu2O impregnation is uniform on the surface of the MWCNTs. However, an increase in the Cu2O loading to 50% causes the agglomeration of particles (shown in Fig. 3(c)). Four sides of the tetrahedral structure of the Cu2O (111) crystal lattice on the surface of the MWCNTs are highlighted in blue lines in Fig. 3 (b) and (c). This Cu2O crystal phase in the Cu2O-based catalysts was found to favor the production of methanol [42]. EDX analysis indicates the presence of carbon with copper and oxygen.
[43][44]. Other diffraction peaks at 36.7 o , 42.5 o , 61.6 o , and 73.9 o are attributed to Cu2O (111), (200), (220), and (311) planes, respectively. The mean particle size was calculated using the
Scherrer’s equation with reference to the line broadening of the strongest diffraction peak
corresponding to Cu2O (111) at 36.7°.

4.3 Thermogravimetric Analysis (TGA)
The samples were subjected to TGA to investigate their thermal degradation temperature and
determine their purity by analyzing the residues left after TGA analyses. Analysis was performed
under air by ramping the temperature of 10 mg of each sample placed in an alumina sample holder from room temperature to 890 o C at a rate of 10 o C/min. The oxidation of the functionalized MWCNTs takes place at 520 o C as shown in Fig. 5. The oxidation of carbon in the electrocatalyst supported on the MWCNTs occurs at a temperature around 420 o C for all
loadings. This confirms that the electrocatalyst is less thermally stable compared to the as-
received MWCNTs. This is due to the incorporation of Cu2O in the MWCNTs enhancing the electronic properties of the electrocatalyst, thereby lowering the temperature at which the support
oxidizes. However, this is not a concern in the experiments described here as they are conducted
below the oxidation temperatures. Residue of each sample was characterized by EDX analysis
and the results indicate that copper metal is present in all loaded samples.

4.4 Raman Spectroscopy
As anchoring of Cu2O at the defect sites of MWCNTs increases the electron flow, thereby increasing the current density, it is essential to determine the location of Cu2O on the functionalized MWCNTs [45]. Raman spectroscopy is used to identify the sites of metal oxide
on the functionalized MWCNTs based on the vibrational mode of the molecules [45]. Two main peaks around 1350 cm -1 and 1575 cm -1 were observed for the MWCNTs sample, as shown in
The other peak around 1575 cm -1 represents the G-band, a symmetrical surface vibration on
graphite that originates from the ordered structure [46]. The ratio of the intensity of the D-band
to G-band (Id/Ig) corresponds to the defect density of a carbon nanotube sample [47]–[49]. The ratio of intensity (Id/Ig) of the Cu2O-MWCNTs samples (1.16) is lower than that of the functionalized MWCNTs sample (1.85). This decrease in intensity ratio indicates that the
nanoparticles of Cu2O anchor at the defect sites rather than at the smooth and ordered surfaces of the MWCNTs. The chemical attachment of Cu2O at the defect sites on MWCNTs improves the electron flow at the surface, favoring the adsorption of OH ions on the surface and ultimately the
reduction of CO2 to methanol.
Fig. 6. Raman spectra of the functionalized MWCNTs and 30% Cu2O-MWCNTs
4.5 Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM)
TEM was performed for the Cu2O loadings of 10% (Fig. 7 (a)) and 30 % (Fig. 7 (b)), in addition to the un-impregnated MWCNTs (Fig. 7 (C)). A tube-like structure with a 10-30 nm outer
diameter was measured for all three samples of MWCNTs. The TEM image of the un-
impregnated MWCNTs shows particles of the catalyst used for the synthesis of the MWCNTs
remaining inside the tubes. Multiwall layers around the catalyst particles are also visible in Fig
7(c). In Fig 7 (a) and (b) these catalyst particles can be clearly distinguished from the black
agglomerations of Cu2O. The TEM images confirm the attachment of Cu2O nanoparticles to the MWCNTs. However, an increase in the loading from 10 to 30 % increases the particle size,
which becomes clear when the size of Cu2O particles in the two images is compared. The particle size determined for the two Cu2O loadings is in agreement with that obtained from XRD characterization.
Fig. 7. TEM images of the MWCNTs (a) impregnated with 10% Cu2O (b) impregnated with 30% Cu2O and (c) un-impregnated
4.6 BET Surface Area Measurement and N2 Adsorption Isotherms
Nitrogen adsorption-desorption isotherms for 10 and 20% cuprous oxide loaded MWCNTs are
shown in Fig. 8 (a) and (b). All isotherms belong to the typical type 3 adsorption model
according to the IUPAC system, which indicates that loading the MWCNTs with Cu2O does not significantly affect the pore size distribution. The BET surface area of the functionalized
MWCNTs and the MWCNTs impregnated with Cu2O is listed in Table 2. The results indicate that an increase in the Cu2O loading increases the size of the particles and decreases the surface area of the catalysts.

4.7 Electrochemical Evaluation 4.7.1 Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV)
LSV was conducted using a two-compartment polycarbonate electrochemical cell to evaluate
the performance of the Cu2O-MWCNTs electrocatalyst with different Cu2O loadings. Prior to performing LSV for the electrocatalyst, the electrochemical reduction of pure copper foil was
studied in 0.5 M NaHCO3 +N2 and NaHCO3 +CO2 electrolyte solutions in a potential range of - 0.2 to -1.8 V. The current density-voltage curves recorded are shown in Fig. 9. Blank copper
foil does not undergo any physical changes in both cases, which confirms the stability of the
electrode. In the electrolyte solution without CO2, the current density is only due to the hydrogen evolution reaction. However, in the case of the CO2 saturated electrolyte, both CO2 reduction and hydrogen evolution occur (reactions (5) and (6) respectively).

These two reactions compete with each other [50]–[52]. Hydrogen evolution consumes electrons and lowers the CO2 reduction. Under N2 saturation, the current density is 0.004 A-cm - 2 at -1.4 V, while under CO2 saturation, the current density is 0.006 A-cm -2 at -1.4V. The observed higher value of current density in the CO2 saturated electrolyte is in agreement with results reported in the literature [50]–[53]. However, there are studies that report higher current
densities in the N2 saturated electrolyte [54]–[57]. The higher current density recorded in the CO2 saturated electrolyte confirms that the copper foil is electrocatalytically active for CO2 reduction.
The current densities of the functionalized MWCNTs and the electrocatalyst with different
loadings of Cu2O (10 to 50 %) were recorded in the potential range of -0.2 V to -1.8 V to evaluate the performance of the electrocatalyst. The current density increases with increasing
potential for all examined samples as shown in Fig. 9. The results indicate that the highest
current density is observed for an optimal loading of 30% Cu2O for the entire potential range. Moreover, supporting Cu2O on the MWCNTs increases the active surface area and the accessibility of the reactants to the active sites within the pores. The presence of the MWCNTs
not only offers reaction sites for CO2, but also traps electrons, increasing the rate of conversion of the intermediates of CO2 - to more useful products. Higher availability of electrons with surface bound protons increases the current density, which in turn result in a higher CO2 reduction at lower potentials. The current density decreases when the Cu2O loading is increased above 30%, as observed for 40% and 50% Cu2O loadings on the MWCNTs in Fig. 9. This decrease in the current density can be attributed to the formation of agglomerates as the
crystallite size increases, which was confirmed by TEM, SEM, and XRD results. In addition,
the lower accessibility of the electrocatalyst at higher loadings, the lower surface energy due to
the decrease in the surface area, and the presence of clusters of particles when the Cu2O loading is high are also responsible for the decrease of the current density.
Fig. 9. Linear sweep voltammetry profiles of pure copper foil, and copper foil coated with the functionalized MWCNTs and Cu2O-impregnated MWCNTs.

sections.heading: 4.7.2 Chronoamperometric determination of the stability of the electrocatalyst
sections.text:
The analysis was performed at a constant voltage of -0.8 V for 1200 seconds. This voltage was
selected as it gave the highest faradaic efficiency for the reduction of CO2 to methanol over 30% Cu2O-MWCNTs (shown in Section 4.7.3). Fig.10 shows the variation of the current density with time during the electrochemical reduction of CO2 at electrodes coated with the electrocatalyst containing varying Cu2O loadings. Initially a decrease in the current density, followed by a steady state response, is observed for all tested samples. This decrease in the current density at an
early stage may be due to the physical detachment of Cu2O, which has been reported in the literature [54]. Fig. 10 shows that 30% Cu2O loaded MWCNTs exhibit the highest activity for
CO2 reduction. The high current density observed for the MWCNTs impregnated with 30% Cu2O is in agreement with the LSV results described earlier, which shows that the current density of -0.0075 A-cm -2 at the beginning decreases to -0.006 A-cm -2 . The current density is
almost constant for all Cu2O loadings after 300 seconds, and the electrolyte solution was clear and transparent after 1200 seconds. This is an indication that significant side reactions are not
occurring in the solution during the entire experiment. The reproducibility of these stability tests
confirms that the MWCNTs impregnated with Cu2O catalysts are stable under the experimental conditions used. A decrease in the current density was observed for the 40% and 50% Cu2O loadings due to the formation of agglomerates, similar to the LSV experiments. As all tested
samples with different loadings of Cu2O are stable in the chronoamperometric experiments, the results also confirm that the agglomeration at high loadings only affects the activity of the
catalyst.
Fig. 10. Chronoamperometric curves of the MWCNTs impregnated with Cu2O at a constant potential of -0.8 V for 1200 sec in CO2 saturated NaHCO3 electrolyte.

sections.heading: 4.7.3 Faradaic efficiency of methanol formation
sections.text:
Chronoamperometry was used to calculate the faradaic efficiency of 30% Cu2O-MWCNTs to study the conversion of CO2 to methanol at different applied potentials. Each potential was applied for 1200 seconds followed by the withdrawal of a 10 ml sample of the electrolyte
solution for the determination of the methanol concentration. Methanol concentration was
determined using gas chromatography with an internal standard using an Agilent Technologies
7890 B gas chromatograph equipped with an FID detector. Faradaic efficiency of methanol was
calculated using the following equation:
(7)
where m is the number of moles of methanol formed as determined by GC, F is the Faraday’s
constant, n is the number of electrons involved in the methanol formation reaction, which is 6, I
is the total current, and t is the time in seconds. Fig. 11 shows that FE depends on the potential
applied in the CO2 reduction. The FE for methanol production increases with increasing potential, and the highest amount of methanol was produced at a potential of -0.8 V with a
maximum FE of 38%. However, methanol formation declined significantly at potentials more
negative of -1.2 V.
The XRD characterization of all Cu2O-MWCNTs catalysts confirmed the presence of a Cu2O (111) phase. This Cu2O (111) phase is believed to facilitate the adsorption of reaction intermediates on the surface of the catalyst, which favors the formation of methanol [58], [59].
When the potential is made more negative, the energy supplied to the electrode will increase the
flow of electrons from the valence band to the conduction band of Cu2O. Electron availability favors the adsorption of OH ions, leading to the formation of methanol at the electrode surface.
However, at potentials more negative of -0.8 V Cu2O is reduced to CuO, leading to a drop in the methanol production as CuO has a lower band gap compared to Cu2O. Furthermore, Cu + is stabilized by the incorporation of Cu2O in the MWCNTs matrix. The MWCNTs support not only stabilizes Cu + , but also prevents Cu + from converting to Cu 2+ and Cu 0 . These properties of the
30% Cu2O-MWCNTs electrocatalyst used in this study led to a higher FE for methanol production at lower potentials compared to catalysts reported in the literature [15], [16], [27],
[50]–[52], [54], [60]–[63].
Fig. 11. Faradaic efficiency of methanol formation after 1200 seconds for 30% Cu2O-MWCNTs determined by chronoamperometry

sections.heading: 5. Conclusions
sections.text:
Functionalized MWCNTs impregnated with varying loadings of cuprous oxide were investigated
for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to methanol. Linear sweep voltammetry shows high current densities for all Cu2O loadings in the potential range of -0.2 to -1.8 V. The electrocatalyst with 30% Cu2O-MWCNTs provides the highest current density in the entire potential range. Supporting Cu2O on the MWCNTs increases the active surface area and the accessibility of the reactants to the active sites within the pores. The presence of the MWCNTs not only offers
reaction sites for CO2, but also traps electrons that increases the rate of conversion of the intermediates of CO2 - to more useful products. Higher Cu2O loadings (40 and 50%) produce lower current densities due to the agglomeration of Cu2O and the crystallite size growth, which leads to a decrease in the surface area and active sites. A faradaic efficiency of 38% was
achieved for 30% Cu2O-MWCNTs at a potential of -0.8 V for the reduction of CO2 to methanol.
The XRD results of all Cu2O-MWCNTs catalysts confirm the presence of the Cu2O (111) crystal phase, which facilitates the adsorption of reaction intermediates on the catalyst surface and
favors the formation of methanol at low potentials. The impregnation of Cu2O on the MWCNTs improved the stability of the catalyst for all examined loadings. The electrocatalyst at all
compositions tested is stable for 1200 sec without any side reactions detected at the highest
methanol formation potential of -0.8 V. These findings show that Cu2O supported on MWCNTs is a promising electrocatalyst for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to methanol with relatively low energy consumption.
